title: Ripples in Water, Ripples in Space

pages.text: Drop a stone into a still pond. Circles spread outwards across the water until they touch the bank. Now watch a leaf floating on the surface. As each ripple passes, the leaf bobs up and down, but it does not travel to the bank with the circles. This simple sight holds a big idea. The water itself is not moving outwards. Only the disturbance is. A wave is a disturbance that carries energy from one place to another without carrying matter along with it. Sound, light, radio signals, and earthquakes all travel as waves.

Now watch a leaf floating on the surface.
As each ripple passes, the leaf bobs up and down, but it does not travel to the bank with the circles.
This simple sight holds a big idea.
The water itself is not moving outwards.
Only the disturbance is.
A wave is a disturbance that carries energy from one place to another without carrying matter along with it.
Sound, light, radio signals, and earthquakes all travel as waves.
pages.alt: Circles spreading across a still pond from the spot where a stone fell, with a leaf floating on the surface.

pages.text: Every wave can be measured. The highest point is the crest, and the lowest point is the trough. The wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next. The amplitude is the height of a crest above the rest position: a bigger amplitude means the wave carries more energy. The frequency is the number of waves that pass a point each second, and it is measured in hertz (Hz). These measurements are tied together by one equation: wave speed = frequency × wavelength. If 2 waves pass each second and each is 3 metres long, the wave travels at 6 metres per second.

These measurements are tied together by one equation: wave speed = frequency × wavelength.
If 2 waves pass each second and each is 3 metres long, the wave travels at 6 metres per second.
pages.alt: A side view of a wave with the crest, trough, wavelength, and amplitude labelled.

pages.text: Waves come in two kinds. Shake one end of a skipping rope up and down and humps run along it. The rope moves up and down while the wave moves forward. This is a transverse wave, and water ripples and light are of this kind. Now push and pull the end of a long spring. Squeezed and stretched sections travel along it, in the same line as your push. This is a longitudinal wave, and sound is of this kind. Most waves need something to travel through, such as water, rope, or air. Light is special: it can cross empty space.

Now push and pull the end of a long spring.
Squeezed and stretched sections travel along it, in the same line as your push.
This is a longitudinal wave, and sound is of this kind.
Most waves need something to travel through, such as water, rope, or air.
Light is special: it can cross empty space.
pages.alt: A skipping rope being shaken into humps, above a long spring with squeezed and stretched sections.

pages.text: In 1916, Albert Einstein predicted a far stranger wave. He had worked out that space is not just emptiness. It can be stretched and squeezed, a little like the surface of a pond. When very heavy objects, such as two black holes, circle each other and crash together, they should send ripples through space itself. These are gravitational waves. They travel at the speed of light. But Einstein doubted that anyone would ever detect them. By the time a gravitational wave reaches Earth, it stretches and squeezes everything by an amount far smaller than a single atom.

pages.text: Scientists built a machine to try. It is called LIGO, and it has two stations in the United States, about 3,000 kilometres apart. Each is shaped like a giant letter L, with two arms 4 kilometres long. A laser beam is split in two and sent along both arms to mirrors and back. If a gravitational wave passes, one arm becomes very slightly longer while the other becomes shorter, and the returning beams no longer match. On 14 September 2015, both stations recorded the same tiny wobble. It came from two black holes that had collided about 1.3 billion years earlier.

pages.alt: A view from above of a detector with two long straight arms meeting at a right angle in open country.

pages.text: The discovery won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2017. Since then, detectors in Italy and Japan have joined the search, and using several stations together helps to show where in the sky a wave came from. By May 2026, the teams had recorded 390 gravitational wave signals, most of them from pairs of black holes. Until 2015, almost everything we knew about the universe came from light and other rays. Black holes give out no light, so they were hidden. Gravitational waves let us study them for the first time. From a pond ripple to a ripple in space, the same ideas apply.

activities.question: What does a wave carry from place to place?
A wave has a frequency of 5 Hz and a wavelength of 2 m. What is its speed?
Which statement about sound waves is correct?
options: They are transverse and can cross empty space
They are longitudinal and need something to travel through
They are the same as water ripples

activities.question: Apply it: Why are gravitational waves so useful for studying black holes?
options: Black holes give out no light, but their collisions send out gravitational waves
Gravitational waves are easier to see with the eye than light
Black holes are close to Earth

activities.prompt: Put the story of gravitational waves in order.
items: Two black holes collide far away in space
The discovery wins a Nobel Prize
The number of recorded signals reaches 390

glossary.definition: A disturbance that carries energy from place to place without carrying matter.
The distance from one crest to the next.
The height of a crest above the rest position.
The number of waves that pass a point each second, measured in hertz.
Transverse wave: a wave in which the movement is at right angles to the direction the wave travels.
Longitudinal wave: a wave in which the movement is along the direction the wave travels.
Gravitational wave: a ripple in space made when very heavy objects move or collide.
